articles.headline: No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record
keyFacts: The current Champions League season has set a record with 187 goals scored at an average of 4.16 per game.
Football analysts stated that the new 36-team format and lack of early jeopardy encourage teams to play more expansively.
Highlights will be broadcast on BBC iPlayer, the BBC Sport app, and BBC One.
body: - Published
More teams, more games - and more goals.
Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite club competition has delivered all of the above and more.
Especially the goals part.
Already trending upwards over the past two campaigns, there has been a genuine goals boom in this year's competition.
The 187 goals scored so far have come at an average of 4.16 per game - the highest in Champions League history.
"Look how many goals have been scored, it's phenomenal," ex-Manchester United and England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "The attackers are being clinical."
Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock described the volume of goals as "incredible" - so how unusual is it?
What the stats say
Ready for lots of numbers?
Not only is the current goals-per-game percentage the highest ever in the Champions League, it is the third highest in European Cup history - behind only 1959-60 (4.19) and 1955-56 (4.38).
While 40 goals were scored across nine games on Tuesday, last week was even more spectacular.
Last Wednesday saw the third highest-scoring day in Champions League history (46 goals), bettered only by the final league-phase matchdays of 2024-25 and 2025-26, when 18 matches took place.
The 78 goals scored across Tuesday and Wednesday last week made matchday two the highest scoring in history.
That was nine more than the total scored on matchday one this season (69) - which, at the time, was the second highest-scoring matchday since the new league phase was introduced in 2024-25.
Will we see the record fall again this week? It's already halfway there.
More entertainment = more quality?

Ever since Uefa announced its plans to alter the format of the Champions League in 2021, the impact on matches has been a hot topic. Scrutiny has only increased since the changes were implemented in time for the 2024-25 season.
After beginning life as a six-team invitational tournament in 1955-56 before growing to a 32-team knockout tournament in 1967, the Champions League as we know it began in 1992.

A group stage was added, with the last 16 entering a knockout phase. There was a brief spell with two group stages, but this was reverted back to the single group-stage format for the 2003-04 tournament.
The group stage previously featured 32 teams in eight groups of four, with the top two sides from each of those groups qualifying for the last 16.
For the start of the 2024-25 season, the group stage was replaced with a 36-team league phase, with each side playing eight one-off fixtures instead of six games against three teams.
The top eight finishers qualify directly for the knockout stages, with those placed ninth to 24th entering a two-legged play-off stage.

The bottom eight are eliminated, meaning that after eight matches, 24 sides are still in the competition. Some argue that that creates a lack of jeopardy, which encourages teams to play more expansively.
But do more goals equal better quality?
"I think the entertainment has gone up, although I'm not sure the quality has gone up," The Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If I'm looking at the games it's brilliant to watch and thrilling because the football itself is fantastic - but what do they mean?

"The lack of jeopardy, why would PSG and Barcelona play for a draw, why not go for it? If you need five wins from the eight games you know you've got some margin there. If you lose it's OK. I think the format allows all the teams to loosen up.
"The entertainment value is there but I think you come away from these matches sometimes and still think 'what does it all mean?'. The lack of jeopardy early on does deliver entertainment."
Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app.
There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00.

articles.headline: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
keyFacts: TechCrunch reported that AI lab Anthropic is circulating a draft bill for congressional consideration that proposes blocking AI models under certain catastrophic risk scenarios.

Politico stated that the legislation suggests independent evaluators registered with the U.S. Commerce Department analyze models for potential disasters involving 50 or more deaths or a billion dollars in damage.
An Anthropic spokesperson told Politico that the draft bill reflects proposals from the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has advocated for since June.
body: Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.

It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

articles.headline: Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’
keyFacts: Mozilla cryptography engineering team member Dennis Jackson reported that private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised.
Security researcher Scott Helme stated that eMudhra used extremely simple private keys, including the numbers 4, 56, and 115.
Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple have remediate the issue so their browsers will not rely on the certificates after users install an update.
body: Tragically simple private keys used by a certification authority based in India have been compromised, meaning the 60-million-plus certs it has issued can’t be trusted and necessitating a massive clean-up job.
The CA of concern in this case is called eMudhra, which boasts of having issued over 60 million digital certificates to help usher in a world of digital trust.
The company has instead panicked the world.
News of the company’s errors appeared on Tuesday in a post by Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s cryptography engineering team.

“On Saturday, October 17, at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report from a community member that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had been compromised,” he wrote . “These keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control.”
Or as Cloudflare put it , “an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.”

Jackson has since elaborated on the incident and the response, which has thankfully seen Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple remediate the issue so their browsers won’t rely on the certificates – at least after users install an update. He also reports that eMudhra has revoked the certs, and lists many FOSS projects that have issued updates that mean they won’t recognize certs from eMudhra.

That’s welcome, but sadly certs signed with these private keys are still out there and many services rely on them. Browser makers are set up to detect and reject bad certs. Others who relied on them may not be, and will likely need to dig into their environments to see if they rely on certs signed by eMudhra. Developer Geoffrey Huntley has offered some advice on automating that process.
At the time of writing, eMudhra has not responded to The Register ’s inquiries about the incident and its security practices.
The latter question is of great interest because security researcher Scott Helme analyzed eMudhra’s certs and found one the private keys it used “is the number 4.”

“Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4... Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second,” Helme wrote.
Other researchers have found private keys including the numbers 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237.
Those are vastly inadequate keys, because they’re easy to guess, making all certs issued by eMudhra susceptible to brute force attacks.
As Helme put it: “A P-384 private key should be a random 384-bit number, which gives you 2³⁸⁴ possibilities (or roughly 10¹¹⁵), so nobody is ever going to search that.”
This is a developing story and The Register will update it as more information becomes available. ®

articles.headline: Investigation Reveals How TikTok Executives Ignored Internal Child-Safety Warnings
keyFacts: Court documents from an ongoing multistate trial reveal that TikTok executives repeatedly ignored internal staff warnings regarding child safety and age restrictions.
The NPR report states that underage users accessed adult features like live video streaming, with TikTok reportedly profiting from the sexual exploitation of minors.
A TikTok spokesperson stated that the NPR report cherry-picked information to mislead the public and ignored documents demonstrating the company's youth safety commitments.
body: Court documents on some of the inner workings of TikTok paint a picture of a tech company repeatedly warned by its own staff about the dangers its platform posed to minors — and then ignoring many of those warnings.

According to an investigation from NPR, unsubmitted depositions from an ongoing multistate trial against TikTok, Meta, Google and Snap reveal that TikTok executives knew that underage users were circumventing its age restrictions. Internal documents also reportedly show that some minors were engaging in sexually exploitative acts using TikTok’s own platform features, including its Live video streaming tool.

The NPR report cites the deposition of Reagan Maher, who worked in safety at the company in the early 2020s, addressing the fallout from a damning 2022 Forbes story about child exploitation on the platform. Maher said she informed senior leaders at the company that kids aged 13 to 15 were accessing features meant for adults, such as monetized live video.
More from CNET

A spokesperson for TikTok told CNET in an email that the information in the NPR report was “clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works.”

TikTok also said that NPR ignored “numerous documents and resources” that would demonstrate how the story’s claims mischaracterize the platform’s features. The spokesperson stated that the company has spent significant amounts of money on safety and introduced over 50 default protections for young users, including Family Pairing tools for parents, and that it was steadfast in its “commitment to the well-being of our community.”
Child-safety reckoning on tech platforms

TikTok is one of a growing group of major tech platforms that have faced lawsuits, scrutiny from parents and financial penalties over how they regulate the safety of younger users. Others include the gaming platform Roblox, AI companies such as OpenAI, streaming video services like Google-owned YouTube and social media companies such as Meta.

Online dangers like predators, cyberbullying and inappropriate content aren’t the only risks for kids. Tech companies are also facing lawsuits for making their platforms addictive and harmful to young users. In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement over those issues in a landmark lawsuit brought on by multiple US states.

TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance — which still holds a stake in the company despite some government-mandated divestment to the US for its American operations — were sued in 2024 by the Department of Justice over violations of child privacy laws, resulting in a $400 million settlement. Last month, TikTok settled a $100 million lawsuit in Alabama and agreed to limit daily child usage in the state.

The NPR report shows not only that TikTok was made aware of these problems by its own staff. It also reveals that the company — among other alleged violations of the law — may have directly profited from the sexual exploitation of minors. Youth were reportedly rewarded with gifts online that could be converted to cash, with TikTok earning a cut of those profits.
Devastating, but predictable
Child-safety advocates told CNET that the NPR report exposes safety gaps in the way platforms such as TikTok were designed.

“These court documents are nothing short of devastating, but for those of us fighting child exploitation every day, they are tragically predictable,” said Michael Medoro, chief operating officer of Childhelp, which focuses specifically on online safety.
Medoro said that active monitoring, the elimination of safety loopholes and stronger age verification will require cooperation between tech leaders, advocates and law enforcement.

According to Shanna Marzilli, CEO of Plan USA, an advocacy group for girls that is part of Plan International, the TikTok documents confirm what young people, especially girls, have been saying for many years. “Online spaces are not safe for them,” she said.

Marzilli said that young people are clued into the idea that tech companies can’t protect them. In a research study conducted among US young people aged 10 to 19, only 14% of them trust social media companies to take sexual harassment and assault seriously.
“Voluntarily implemented parental controls and self-reported age limits are demonstrably ineffective when platforms leave these structural loopholes open,” Marzilli said.

articles.headline: Meet the California multimillionaires demanding the billionaire tax become law
keyFacts: A group of more than 40 wealthy Californians signed an open letter urging voters to approve Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on state billionaires.
Signatories including Disney scion Tim Disney and Men's Wearhouse founder George Zimmer argued the tax would prevent millions of Californians from losing health care.
A spokesperson for the opposing billionaires group, Building a Better California, declined to comment.
body: The increasingly cantankerous fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax is now pitting the .01% against the .001%, as a group of multimillionaires call out their even richer counterparts for not paying more taxes.

Disney scion Tim Disney, Men’s Wearhouse founder George Zimmer and former San Francisco congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti — a mere centimillionaire as one of the founding engineers of Stripe — are among more than 40 wealthy Californians who signed an open letter urging voters to approve Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on the state’s billionaires.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
“As multimillionaires, we’re willing to do our part,” the letter says. “It’s past time for billionaires — our thousand millionaire cousins — to do theirs.”

The letter by Patriotic Millionaires and Tax the Ultra-Rich Now supports a 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. Others who signed on include documentary filmmaker Matthew Cooke and virtual reality pioneer Jaron Lanier.
Chakrabarti has been particularly pointed in defending the labor-sponsored wealth tax, dismissing warnings that it would send California’s richest residents fleeing for other states.

“I think the disappointing thing is how few of the people who have made their wealth because of everything California has given them are willing to do the bare minimum to keep 3.4 million people from losing Medicaid,” Chakrabarti told The California Post in a text message.

“My thoughts on Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt and others is this: all of you are probably going to make about 30% returns on your money this year, based on what returns for billionaires have been over the last several years. You won’t even notice a 5% wealth tax — you’ll still be richer next year than you were this year.”
He added, “But over 3 million Californians will have their lives changed. Do you really want your legacy to be that you fought tooth and nail against that?”
Disney, a filmmaker and author, cast the measure as a response to federal health care cuts and a fight over whose interests government serves.
“Prop 40 is about dignity, decency, and fairness,” Disney said in a statement.
He argued that the tax would help prevent millions of Californians from losing health care following cuts under President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
A spokesperson for the billionaires group fighting the wealth, Building a Better California, delcined comment Tuesday.
The millionaires group released findings from a YouGov poll of California millionaires that they said showed 57% support for Prop. 40.
Roughly 60% of those polled supported higher taxes on people with extreme wealth if the proceeds went to state health and education programs, according to a news release.
Another 56% said they would not leave California if asked to pay a little more in taxes, while 78% agreed billionaires have too much influence in state elections.
The release did not include the survey’s sample size, field dates or margin of error.
“If there’s a price tag on our beaches, our mountains, our piers, our cable cars, our forests, and our state parks, we’re proud to pay it,” the letter says.
Rather than letting the billionaires eat their cake, the millionaires seem ready for a food fight.

articles.headline: Trump says he will have spent $400m to support Republicans in midterms – US politics live
keyFacts: Donald Trump said his political operation and aligned super PAC will have spent $400m supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections.
Trump cited his party support and claimed the investment was needed to prevent French-style civil unrest if Democrats win control of Congress.
Trump will continue his midterm campaign blitz with an upcoming rally scheduled in Greenville, North Carolina.
body: Trump says he will have spent $400m to support Republican candidates in midterms
Donald Trump said that he will have spent $400m supporting Republican candidates in midterm races by the time election day rolls around on 3 November.
The staggering amount will be spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc.

“More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more. It is my Great Honor to do so on behalf of the Republican Party, which has done so much to bring our Country back from the Edge of Oblivion,” he wrote on Truth Social.

He cited his belief in the Republican party, but also the riots that have swept through France, as his reasons behind the spend. A reminder, Trump has repeated baseless claims that the demonstrations, which have descended into chaos and seen thousands arrested, are the result of mass migration.

Trump loyalist and rightwing influencer Laura Loomer tore into the Department of Justice on Tuesday, saying the agency was belittling veterans, who were exposed to contaminated drinking water at a Marine Corps base decades ago, with “lowball” settlement offers.

“This is a political disaster waiting to happen. Let’s be clear: Democrats are 100% going to weaponize this against President Trump and try to hurt him with veterans heading into the midterms in two weeks,” Loomer wrote in a X post, blaming associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr.
In a thinly-veiled rebuff, attorney general Todd Blanche appeared to suggest Loomer’s diatribe was financially-motivated.
“You should be transparent with your followers, and you are dead wrong about Stanley,” he responded on X.
“We love our veterans and we want to get these cases right. Find a different obsession other than going after one of DOJ’s best fighters.”
Loomer shot back, saying Trump wanted to fire Woodward, but took pity on him “because his lefty wife is divorcing him,” she claimed.

Some outlets, including Bloomberg, reported earlier this year that Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general in the DOJ’s civil rights division, would be promoted to Woodward’s post. She was not.
Trump's use of an antisemitic slur for a second time draws belated, indirect criticism from ADL

The Anti-Defamation League, which calls itself the world’s “leading anti-hate organization”, founded in 1913 “to protect the Jewish people”, denounced the use of the term “shylock” as antisemitic on Tuesday, without explaining that the slur had been used one day earlier by Donald Trump in a speech in Kansas.

The ADL’s brief social-media post made no mention of Trump at all and offered no explanation as to why the group found it necessary to explain, today, that anyone equating an avaricious person to Shylock, the villainous Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice, is using an antisemitic trope.

“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the ADL posted on X but not its other social media accounts. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”

Critics who accuse the ADL of using accusations of antisemitism selectively, to attack people who are critical of Israel, suggested that the Jewish-American civil rights group was going easy on Trump because of his support for Israel.

Matt Duss, a former foreign police adviser to senator Bernie Sanders, the most prominent Jewish American politician, responded to the ADL’s failure to mention Trump by suggesting its president would have been more direct had someone else used the slur. “If a Democrat said it Jonathan Greenblatt would be knocking people over to get in front of a camera to condemn them by name, but it was Trump so it’s just a general public service announcement,” Duss wrote.

In 2014, after then vice-president Joe Biden described people who take financial advantage of American service members as “shylocks”, the Anti-Defamation League’s national director accepted his apology and called the remarks “a teachable moment”.
Trump’s use of the slur, at a rally in Kansas on Monday night, came just one day after he had endorsed Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Monday, ahead of Israel’s elections.

Trump invoked the antisemitic stereotype as part of his defense of the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, a doctor who has been criticized for filing lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills, leading to 18 of them being arrested.
The president began by claiming, falsely, that Marshall had been required by law to take legal action over unpaid bills, even one for just $101.

Marshall, Trump told supporters at a rally outside Wichita on Monday, “was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people.” There is, in fact, no such law.

Turning to Marshall’s critics, including his Democratic rival, Adam Hamilton, who featured some of Marshall’s patients in a campaign ad, Trump said: “they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy.”

“If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said again, repeating the falsehood he based his defense on. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability,” the president claimed, falsely.

Trump’s use of the antisemitic slur came 15 months after he was made aware of its meaning when he used it at a rally in Iowa. Speaking on 3 July 2025, Trump Trump told supporters that eliminating the taxes on inherited family farms would save farmers from “going to the banks and borrowing from, in some cases a fine banker, and in some cases shylocks and bad people”.

The day after that Iowa rally, the ADL called the president’s use of the term “very troubling and irresponsible”, but Trump claimed ignorance when he was asked by a reporter if he had intended to use the word “shylocks” to refer to Jews.

“No, I’ve never heard it that way,” Trump replied then. “To me, a shylock is somebody that’s a, uh, a moneylender at high rates. I’ve never heard it that way. You view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.”

Donald Trump said that he will have spent$400m supporting Republican candidates in midterm races by the time election day rolls around on 3 November. The staggering amount will have been spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc. The president will continue his campaign blitz with a rally in Greenville, North Carolina on Tuesday.

Beyond Washington, Trump’s special envoys – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – wrapped up a meeting with Nordic leaders and Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo. The Ukrainian president said that the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow. Witkoff is set to head to St Petersburg on Wednesday to relay to the new peace proposals discussed with Ukraine to Moscow.

Zelenskyy also said that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine is working again, after sustained disruptions. Earlier, the Ukrainian president said he had a “substantive conversation” with US secretary of state Marco Rubio.

Meanwhile, Rubio told reporters in India today that “there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine”. He called the assertion that people in Ukraine are dying because the US is denying them information “scandalous” and “outrageous”. However, in an interview with CNN, representative Eugene Vindman, the Democratic congressman from Virginia, slammed the secretary of state’s comments. “He [Rubio] is lying and so is the president when they say that they are not restricting intelligence in violation of the law,” Vindman said.

And Trump continued to blame the riots in France on mass migration, without providing any evidence. “It’s an immigration problem. You have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that,” Trump said. Even though French authorities have not tied the upheaval to immigrants, that hasn’t deterred the president from insisting that similar chaos would be the US’ fate if Democrats win control of Congress in the upcoming midterms.
Also in the Oval Office today, Mehmet Oz – the director of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the health department would be deferring $1.2bn more to California.
This comes after the Trump administration already paused almost $1bn in Medicaid funding to the Golden state in July.

“They just got the note, and we’re doing that because the growth of personal care services in California,” Oz told reporters on Tuesday. “That one little area where you’re paying someone to carry groceries upstairs for your mom, which many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, I would think. But in California, they’ll pay you a lot of money for it, and it’s actually run by the counties. But California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years.”
Once again, Trump launched into a racist attack against Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, and the Somali-American community.

This comes after the justice department launched a raid on the Minnesota representative’s Washington DC home. Reports citing sources familar with the probe said the search earlier this month was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child. The raid has been met with widespread condemnation, particularly so close to the midterm elections.
However, Trump today doubled down.
“I think she’s a sick, a very dishonest person, but who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It’s a real shit house,” he said.

“Somalians vote for her … Most of them shouldn’t be here. You know, they have like a 98 % unemployment rate. They don’t work,” the president added, an incredible statistic given the fact that the census doesn’t actually track the unemployment rate for Somali-Americans specifically.

Donald Trump was not optimistic about whether peace talks appear to be back on the table ahead of Steve Witkoff’s meeting in St Petersburg, Russia tomorrow (following his summit with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nordic leaders in Oslo).

“Russia is a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that’s what they’ve done. They’ve taken a very large piece of land, and you know you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week,” Trump said, before repeating his insistence for Zelenskyy to cut a deal.

“We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve got nothing back, other than high diesel,” Trump said, without acknowledging that the price of diesel and gasoline jumped at the beginning of the Iran war in February. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal … In my opinion, it’s just really just going to get worse.”
On France, the president once again said – without providing any evidence – that the riots are due to mass migration.
“It’s an immigration problem. You have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that,” Trump said.

However, the French authorities have not tied the upheaval to immigrants, but that hasn’t deterred the president for insisting that the chaos would be a fate the US is destined for if Democrats win control of Congress in the upcoming midterms.
Donald Trump announces incentive program for people to report fraud, after conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley's allegations

In the Oval Office, Trump announced an incentive program for people to report fraud, in honor of conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley – who, you may remember, posted a video last year alleging fraud by daycare centers servicing Minneapolis’s Somali American community.
The video, initially posted in December, resulted in a deluge of anti-immigrant and anti-Somali content across social media, including in Truth Social posts by Donald Trump.
In July, Fahima Egeh Mahamud, the CEO of the daycare center that appeared in Shirley’s video, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the US.
Under the administration’s proposed program, people who submit information through that results in a fraud conviction could receive up to $30,000.
In the Oval Office today, Trump presented Shirley, 24, with a check for $10,000 for his work.
Trump says he will have spent $400m to support Republican candidates in midterms
Donald Trump said that he will have spent $400m supporting Republican candidates in midterm races by the time election day rolls around on 3 November.
The staggering amount will be spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc.

“More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more. It is my Great Honor to do so on behalf of the Republican Party, which has done so much to bring our Country back from the Edge of Oblivion,” he wrote on Truth Social.

He cited his belief in the Republican party, but also the riots that have swept through France, as his reasons behind the spend. A reminder, Trump has repeated baseless claims that the demonstrations, which have descended into chaos and seen thousands arrested, are the result of mass migration.
Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 – does Adam Hamilton have the courage, brain and heart to cause an extraordinary upset?

Just two years after Donald Trump won Kansas by 16 points in his fight to regain the White House, Republicans in the state are scrambling to retain their dominance. The battle for one of its two seats in the US Senate is too close to call, setting the stage for a potentially extraordinary upset.
Some recent polls even put Democrat Adam Hamilton on course for a historic victory. Kansans have not sent a representative of the party to the US Senate since 1932.

On the campaign trail, Hamilton regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.

Washington needs more of all three, he says, and he can deliver it. He decided to run for office after seeing the Trump administration act in ways that were “not good or kind or compassionate or humble”, Hamilton – in the energetic cadence of the pastor he is – told a crowd of business leaders in Topeka on Friday. He was waiting for Roger Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent senator, to stand up for his state and its people.

“I would have arguments with Roger Marshall in the shower. He was not in the shower with me,” Hamilton joked. “And I would just say, Roger, please stand up for your people. You were not hired to be a spokesperson for the White House. You were hired to fight for your people.”

Hamilton’s role as senior pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation comes with name recognition and speaking skills. But Marshall’s liabilities as his opponent – namely, the fact he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them – have contributed greatly to Hamilton’s prospects of flipping the seat.

Electorally, he’s trying to win over independents and Republicans, calling himself an independent-minded Democrat. It would be valuable, he told the business leaders last week, for Kansas to have a Democrat like him and a Republican in Jerry Moran representing them in the US Senate – working both sides of the aisle.
Mike Bloomberg is donating $80m to Democrats ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Speaking to the New York Times on Tuesday, Bloomberg’s advisor Howard Wolfson said: “He believes in participation in our democracy. And obviously the scale of his participation, given his resources and his means, is greater than other people’s financially. But other people are participating in different ways.”
“He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns,” Wolfson said, adding that Bloomberg “expects a result.”

The outlet reports that the former New York City major, now 84-years old, is focused on securing a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives, with at least $50m of his doantion to be spent on House races.

In response to Bloomberg’s donation, House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries said: “Mayor Bloomberg played an incredibly instrumental role in the decisive midterm election in 2018. The extraordinary support from Mayor Bloomberg will once again help Democrats flip the House,” the outlet reports.

articles.headline: Robinson sparks 23-0 run as Pistons stun Celtics in NBA season opener
keyFacts: Duncan Robinson scored 15 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter to help the Detroit Pistons beat the Boston Celtics 121-113 in the NBA season opener on Tuesday.
The Detroit Pistons used a 23-0 run in the fourth quarter to overcome a deficit after trailing by as many as 22 points earlier in the game.
Paul George scored a game-high 38 points in his debut for the Boston Celtics, while Jalen Duren and Cade Cunningham each scored 22 points for the Pistons.
body: Duncan Robinson scored 15 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter as the Detroit Pistons reeled off 23 unanswered points to beat the visiting Boston Celtics 121-113 in the NBA’s regular-season opener on Tuesday afternoon.
Jalen Duren and Cade Cunningham scored 22 points apiece for the Pistons, who led the Eastern Conference with 60 wins last season.
Javonte Green came off the bench to score 19 points in 18 minutes, while Ausar Thompson added 11 points, 11 rebounds and five assists.

Paul George scored a game-high 38 points on his Celtics debut. Payton Pritchard and Derrick White scored 17 points apiece, but Jayson Tatum was held to 13 points on six-for-23 shooting, although he contributed 11 assists.
The Celtics led by 13 at halftime thanks to a second-quarter surge. Detroit held a 39-35 advantage early in the quarter before Boston reeled off 15 unanswered points.
George scored the Celtics’ final eight points of the half as Boston took a 58-45 lead into the break.
George showed no signs of cooling off in the third quarter, hitting three three-pointers in a 52-second span to give Boston their biggest lead at 72-50.

Green entered the game shortly afterward to slow George down. He not only did that but also gave Detroit an offensive spark, scoring 11 points in the quarter, including three three-pointers, as the Pistons pulled within three in the closing seconds.

George opened the fourth quarter with a layup to give Boston a 90-82 lead. The Celtics soon stretched their advantage to 12 points, but Detroit began another comeback, sparked by a three-point play from Thompson.

Robinson scored 11 straight points to pull the Pistons within one at 99-98. He then set up a three-pointer for Green before Duren converted a three-point play. Robinson hit another three-pointer with 5min 13sec remaining to put Detroit ahead 107-99.
Green capped the 23-0 run with another three-pointer, extending the Pistons’ lead to 112-99 with 3min 33sec left.
Boston rallied to within four points, but Green made two free throws with 6.7 seconds remaining to seal Detroit’s opening-day victory.

articles.headline: Rio Ngumoha breaks Liverpool record and is a major England threat to Bukayo Saka
keyFacts: Rio Ngumoha provided two assists to help Liverpool secure a 4-3 comeback victory over Villarreal in the Champions League.
Jason Cundy claimed that Ngumoha's performance suggests he could challenge Bukayo Saka for a starting right-wing role with England.
The assist for Ronald Araujo made 18-year-old Ngumoha the youngest player to score or assist in the competition for Liverpool.
body: Rio Ngumoha dazzled for Liverpool in their 4-3 victory over Villarreal – and Bukayo Saka should be worried about his England spot.
It’s a suggestion made by Jason Cundy after the teenager picked up two assists in the Champions League thriller at Anfield on Tuesday.
Ngumoha arguably had his best Liverpool performance to date as he assisted two goals in their comeback win over Villarreal Getty
Player-of-the-match Ngumoha provided for Ronald Araujo with a floating cross and then teed up Alexis Mac Allister as Liverpool came from behind to win their third European match of the season.
The teenager has started in all of their Champions League ties and is becoming an integral part of Andoni Iraola’s squad, with a new deal also a possibility .
He featured in England’s pre-World Cup training camp, and made his debut during the 1-0 friendly win over New Zealand.

Thomas Tuchel did not select him as part of his final 26-man squad but, with Euro 2028 the next major tournament, and Cundy believes the starlet is capable of battling Saka for a starting spot on the right.
Ngumoha v Saka for England starting role
When asked if Ngumoha should play right-wing for England , Cundy said on The Sports Bar : “After that performance, you have to be seriously looking at him. He was involved in the last squad.

Cundy added: “He has caught the eye. Every time he plays, he catches the eye. And there are very few players that can do that at his age. But the thing that he’s got, he has the ability because he’s so young.
“There’s no fear of failure. You get this with young players. They don’t know what it’s like. Failure doesn’t exist in their lives. They’ve always been the best.
“They just go out and just go and showcase what you’ve got. Go on, do a step over. Who cares if I get it? And more often than not, because he’s so full of confidence…
“There will be a moment in his career where there will be a dip, he will drop in form. It inevitably happens with most young kids but wow, what a performance, what a player.”

Cundy then claimed that Saka, who is the consistent starter at right-wing for England, may be wary of Ngumoha’s rise as he said: “Saka’s had a lot of injuries, but he’s England’s starter right now in England’s best team.
With 59 caps, Saka has been the long-term go-to choice on the right for England – but Cundy thinks Ngumoha can rival him for the starting role Getty
“But, when you’re watching young players come through, and even though Saka’s still got to reach the peak of his powers…
“When you’re looking over your shoulder, you’re going, ‘Wow, this kid has got something’. Liverpool fans should be very excited, England fans should be very excited.”
Ngumoha with a record-breaking display
Ngumoha and Barcelona star Lamine Yamal are the only two teens in this season’s Champions League to bag two assists in one match.
The cross for Araujo also made Ngumoha the youngest ever player to score or assist in the competition for Liverpool, doing so aged 18 years and 52 days.
In addition, he is the third-youngest Englishman to provide an assist after Jude Bellingham, Lewis Miley and Theo Walcott.
Ngumoha has now made seven Champions League appearances for Liverpool, although he is still waiting for his first competition goal.
Ngumoha broke a club record on what was a night to remember in Liverpool colours on the Champions League stage Getty
“Tonight is up there with one of the best I’ve played I think,” he said in his post-match interview with Amazon Prime. “I enjoyed myself out there, the team helped me a lot…
“Whenever I get the ball and have the opportunity to go one v one, or sometimes two v one, I’ll by all means go for it.
“I believe in myself to do that and the more chances we get the more we can worry the opposition and be ruthless.”
Ngumoha added: “To hear my name being chanted by the crowd is a dream. We have the best fans in the world.”

articles.headline: Judge Trump called a ‘lunatic’ abruptly backs off demand after showdown with DOJ No. 3
keyFacts: Judge Ana Reyes withdrew her demand that Justice Department attorneys add their signatures to a Sunday filing regarding a D.C. golf course dispute.
The hearing followed President Donald Trump calling Reyes a crazed lunatic on social media and accusing her of blocking court audio recordings.
The lawsuit involves a dispute over the Trump administration's removal of hundreds of trees at the federally owned East Potomac Golf Links.
body: A Biden-appointed judge embroiled in a fierce dispute with the Trump administration over the removal of hundreds of trees at a federally owned D. C. golf course reversed course during Monday's nearly seven-hour hearing.

Judge Ana Reyes ended the nearly seven-hour hearing by backing away from her initial demand that Justice Department attorneys arguing the case put their names alongside Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr.’s Sunday filing. Reyes had invoked Rule 11, which requires attorneys to stand behind the factual basis of court filings and can subject them to sanctions for violations.
"Late breaking news," Reyes said. "I'm going to withdraw request that DOJ refile yesterday's brief with identification of who signed it. we've all got better things to spend our time on."

The about-face from Reyes, who hours before the hearing was dubbed a "crazed lunatic" by President Donald Trump on Truth Social, is the latest development in a court battle over Trump's plans to completely renovate East Potomac Golf Links into a "world-class, U.S. Open-caliber course." The lawsuit, which was first filed in February, reached a boiling point earlier this month when the National Park Service removed roughly 430 trees at the golf course over a weekend. The Interior Department said the tree removals were part of a years-old plan to restore the course’s historic design and were unrelated to Trump’s proposed overhaul.
BIDEN JUDGE REJECTS OBAMA CIA CHIEF'S LEGAL BID AGAINST TRUMP OVER ONE KEY PROBLEM

Though the action did not violate a court order, it prompted Reyes to impose a temporary restraining order barring further tree removals. She also was described as "screaming" at the administration attorneys during an Oct. 12 hearing.
The hearing prompted Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward to seek Reyes’ removal from the case , accusing her of bias and "open hostility" toward the Trump administration.
Both Woodward and Trump have called for the release of the court’s audio recordings of the hearings.

"The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane? The tapes have been blocked from usage by the judge," Trump posted Monday hours before the hearing, saying the Trump administration has a "right" to turn the course into a "great, safe, and prestigious" golf course. "Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY! The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C."

Trump made two other tweets Sunday saying that Interior Department Secretary Doug Burgum and architect Tom Fazio had "developed a plan" to revamp the East Potomac Golf Links into a "World Class Championship Golf Course" and that work would begin November 15.

The tweets prompted Reyes to give the Justice Department an 8 p.m. filing deadline, saying Trump's characterization conflicted with a previous filing that stated there was "no agency action" in Trump's golf course plan.
The filing was signed only by Woodward, which immediately became a point of contention at the start of Monday's hearing.
LIBERAL LAW PROFESSOR BREAKS WITH OBAMA JUDGE OVER TRUMP LAWYER CRACKDOWN: ‘I REFUSE TO TEACH’ IT
Reyes demanded that the attorneys "raise your hand" if they would sign the briefing, which Woodward said was "not an appropriate request."
She then invoked Rule 11 and ordered them to the podium to sign the filing.

But Woodward and the attorneys refused. Reyes initially set a 3 p.m. deadline but later extended it until noon Tuesday and offered to allow the attorneys' names to appear on the brief rather than requiring their signatures. In the end, she abandoned the demand completely.

"For those wondering, a common reason high level DOJ appointees sometimes signs briefs boils down to good leadership," Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor, wrote on X. "If there is something that is likely to be contentious with a judge, a DOJ leader signs their name on the brief so that any issues someone has with the brief is directed at them rather than lower level attorneys. Regardless, it goes without saying that a decision such as this should not be something a judge is inquiring into."
EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S DC JUDICIAL NEMESIS TARGETED IN MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT OVER ALLEGED BIDEN DOJ TIES

"DOJ line attorneys increasingly do not sign briefs because of Dem law fare. Dems have and continue to go after the bar licenses of young DOJ line attorneys who are simply executing on behalf of the department," Rachel Boulvard, vice president of programs at the Conservative Partnership Institute, wrote on X.

Reyes, appointed by President Joe Biden in 2023, previously faced a Justice Department judicial-misconduct complaint over her handling of litigation challenging Trump’s restrictions on transgender individuals serving in the military.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
During a February 2025 hearing, Reyes questioned a Trump administration attorney about what Jesus Christ would say about policies excluding transgender people from homeless shelters.

Then-DOJ Chief of Staff Chad Mizelle accused Reyes of "hostile and egregious misconduct" and potential bias in a formal complaint filed with the D.C. Circuit. The complaint was later dismissed, with the circuit’s chief judge concluding that a recusal motion was the proper avenue for challenging Reyes’ conduct.

articles.headline: Mix ‘Coffin Flop’ With QWOP And You’ve Got A Game That’s At The Top Of My Steam Next Fest List
keyFacts: Fallbearers is a Steam Next Fest demo that combines QWOP with a Coffin Flop sketch premise.
Players control two Victorian pallbearers carrying a casket across hazard-filled streets while managing speed, jumps, and height.
The demo has no release date yet, but the full game will feature varied terrain like snowy landscapes.
body: With an unmanageably colossal heap of demos on offer, a massive number of which look to be filled with AI-generated garbage, the current Steam Next Fest is a serious bummer. How on earth is any adult with limited free time supposed to muck through the stables of slop to find something worthwhile? Increasingly, people have been creating ad hoc slop-free recommendation lists on social media in addition to sharing browser plugins and other tools that people can use to filter out games that have a genAI disclosure. But even with tools to separate the good game wheat from the slop chaff, that’s still a lot of games to sift through, so I’m gonna throw my own recommendation onto the pile with the only demo I’ve made time for this Next Fest: Fallbearers.

I found the game via Bluesky, wooed to its Steam page by the game’s trailer alone. Imagine a game that combines Bennet Foddy’s track-and-field simulator QWOP with the “Coffin Flop” bit from Tim Robinson’s HBO sketch show I Think You Should Leaveâthat’s Fallbearers.

In it, youâby yourself or you with a friendâcontrol two Victorian-era pallbearers as they try to transport the dearly departed from the hearse to the grave. The pallbearers walk on their own, but you have to control how fast they move, when they jump, and how high they hold their precious (but slippery!) load to navigate busy streets filled with manholes, steep inclines, and the occasional malicious bulldog.

Fallbearers‘ demo is criminally short, but I had great time figuring out when and how to raise and lower my two chaps to bear the dead to their final resting place. It’s harder than it looks, but not as hard as it may seem if you’re just one person. Trying to figure it out with two people, though, will likely be a hoot. You can fail a certain number of times depending on the difficulty, but if the corpse flops out of the coffin, game over. The full game promises even more varied terrain including snowy landscapes that necessitate the use of skis. There’s no release date yet, but I suspect it’ll be out sometime between the Sloppy Steaks cooking sim and the Dan Flashes Dressmaker DLC.

articles.headline: Reel out garbage from a flooded planet and make number go up as satisfyingly as you can in the incremental fishing game Selkie's Salvage&Co.
keyFacts: Selkie's Salvage&Co. is an incremental video game where players control a robot to fish trash out of a flooded planet.
Players grind collected garbage to upgrade their fishing gear, boat capabilities, and automation equipment.
A demo is currently available and the full game is scheduled for release on October 27th.
body: The wonderful thing about video games is that they can take something that is, quite frankly, terrible, and turn it into an experience where you can't help but think "just five more minutes." Incremental games often have that effect, and Selkie's Salvage&Co. is no different in that regard, it's just the funny thing is that it is essentially a game about taking your rubbish out.

That is bastardising it. The setting for the world is one where the entire planet is flooded, and you, a robot created by an anthropomorphic rat girl (the titular Selkie) who I can already predict salacious fan art of, have to clean up a whole bunch of trash from it by fishing it out. This starts slow of course, all you have is you, your fishing rod, and a magnetic arm that can't carry all that much. The more trash you collect and feed into a grinder, the more you can steadily increase your capabilities.

You increase your fishing and carrying loads, you add a net to the back of your boat that automatically catches trash for you, you get a gun component that gives you extra points if you manage to shoot the trash you've caught in the air. It is all about maximising your efforts until certain elements of it are automated, of course, all in the name of collecting that sweet, sweet garbage as efficiently as possible. Along the way you may come across some artifacts from the past, things like a basketball or one of those "For Dummies" books about recycling. It's a cute touch, and apparently they provide some mechanical bonuses too, though I didn't manage to grab one in my time with the demo.

Still, Selkie's Salvage&Co. has that satisfying juice all good incremental games do, where your desire to maximise Number Go Up outweighs any semblance of having a good night's sleep. I said it was satisfying, not healthy. In any case, if you too want to hang out with the rat girl while she forces you to collect rubbish, then you can have a go at the demo or at least throw it a wishlist yourself on Steam ahead of its release on October 27th.

articles.headline: Is the US abandoning Ukraine?
keyFacts: President Donald Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to end Russia's invasion and delayed sanctions designed to pressure Russia.
Trump reopened the US market to Russian diesel and demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil refineries to help lower domestic gas prices.
Ukrainian officials said the US campaign to pressure Zelenskyy involved disruptions to intelligence-sharing and satellite internet services.
body: A man clears debris at the site of an air attack in Kyiv on October 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Oleksii Filippov/AFP via Getty Images
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .
You can’t quite say that President Donald Trump is “turning” on Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, because he never truly seemed to have Zelenskyy’s back.

There was that time Trump panned Zelenskyy as a “modestly successful comedian.” Or that excruciating meeting where Trump and Vice President JD Vance harangued Zelenskyy for inadequately “thanking” them.

But over the past week, Trump has dropped even the meager niceties he sort of faked before. On Monday, he blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end Russia’s invasion…and suggested it was time for “somebody else” to take over negotiations.

Three days earlier, he delayed a package of tariffs and other sanctions designed to pressure Russia to end its four-year onslaught in Ukraine. And a week before that, Trump announced — after an apparently chummy phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin — that the US would reopen its market to Russian diesel, reversing a ban imposed shortly after the invasion.
Go a little deeper
View Link

All this diplomatic whiplash comes as Russia continues to bombard Ukraine with drone and missile strikes, killing hundreds of civilians in September alone and leaving hundreds of thousands of people without power. The first two weeks of October ranked among the deadliest periods for civilians in the country since 2022, according to UN monitors.

But while those escalating strikes threaten both human lives and long-standing international norms around territory and sovereignty — norms that actually matter quite a lot to American security, long-term — there’s another issue that Trump is more concerned with right now: Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Those strikes drive up the cost of gas, and those prices are, of course, of profound concern to American voters , who are paying near- record highs for gasoline and diesel fuel (…primarily due to the war in Iran , I am obliged to note). More than any other issue, high living costs threaten to hamstring the GOP in next month’s midterm elections.

Trump has, perhaps predictably, pursued a Russia policy that he says could ease prices at home. In addition to allowing imports of Russian diesel, Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil refineries and ramped up pressure on Zelenskyy to negotiate an end to the war.

According to Ukrainian officials, that campaign has lately involved disruptions to both intelligence-sharing and the US-based satellite internet service Ukraine uses to intercept Russian attacks. (On Tuesday afternoon, Zelenskyy said intel sharing — if not satellite service — had been restored again.)

In either case, it will likely take more than arm-twisting to make the whole situation go away for good. As Vox’s Josh Keating laid out earlier this year , the US does have quite a lot of leverage over Ukraine — and Trump could very well pressure Zelenskyy to accept a peace deal with no real assurance that Russia won’t just invade again.
But we’ve all seen this movie before, as recently as 2014: Without credible guarantees, Putin could catch his breath, regroup, and return to Ukraine in a few months or years to take even more land.

The real, long-term threat there is that a stronger Russia would be even better positioned to menace the rest of Europe. And America’s power could suffer as its allies look elsewhere for less fair-weather friends.
But uh…diesel might be a bit cheaper? Thank God for small mercies, I guess.

articles.headline: Next-Gen Xbox Could Be $1,800 And Launch In 2028 – Report
keyFacts: Fortune reported that Microsoft's Project Helix console could cost between $1,200 and $1,800 and potentially launch in 2028.
The report stated that Microsoft might also release a next-generation Xbox handheld device by the end of 2027.
According to Fortune, more Xbox layoffs are scheduled to occur this month, in November, and in January 2027.
body: A new report sheds more details on Microsoft's plans for new Xbox hardware, including a new handheld device and console, and one of the biggest takeaways is the alleged price.
According to Fortune , the Project Helix console could cost between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft opts to subsidize the cost. The system could launch in 2028, the report said.

It's not uncommon for platform-holders to eat some of the cost of a new console and make up the difference with software and services. When the Xbox Series X and S platforms launched in 2020, then-Xbox CEO Phil Spencer said Microsoft was losing as much as $200 on every console it sold.
Project Helix might be very expensive.

Part of what might be driving up the price for new consoles is the ongoing AI-fueled memory and component shortages. Microsoft itself is one of the biggest proponents of the build-out of all things AI, so its own efforts are contributing to an environment where the next Xbox could be incredibly expensive. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reacted to this irony, saying it's "wonderful" that GPUs have use beyong gaming.
Richer households already made up the majority of console-buyers today , and that trend is expected to continue
Additionally, the report said Microsoft might release a "next-generation handheld device" for Xbox by the end of 2027, though there were no details on pricing or anything else.
Project Helix is the name for Microsoft's efforts for a "family of devices," so that would seemingly span both console and handheld.

The report added that Microsoft's Xbox and Windows teams reportedly battled over what software should run Project Helix, with the Windows team wanting the handheld to use a "trimmed-down" version of Windows Home. The Xbox team, meanwhile, reportedly pushed to build its own dedicated software.

An unnamed "senior Xbox executive" was said to have threatened to pull the plug on the entire handheld device rather than use Windows. Going forward, Xbox is "largely controlling the direction" of the handheld's OS, but Sharma told the site that the two teams work together. "We can't build Helix on our own," she said.

Sharma took over as Xbox CEO in February this year, immediately declaring that Xbox was in an unhealthy place and taking drastic measures that she believes may right the ship, including laying off staff, closing studios, and cancelling games. The layoffs, which have included about 2,000 people so far , are not done yet, as the Fortune story says more Xbox layoffs are coming this month, in November, and then again in January 2027.
Sharma also made major organizational changes, including handing Halo over to Activision for the future .
